result: Human pathway and reaction summations of release 97, read through reactome.org/ContentService on 2026-10-21. Digestion of dietary carbohydrate (R-HSA-189085): salivary and intestinal amylases convert starch to maltotriose, maltose, limit dextrins and some glucose; enzymes on the luminal surface of enterocytes digest limit dextrins and disaccharides to glucose, galactose and fructose; lactose yields glucose and galactose, sucrose glucose and fructose. Intestinal hexose absorption (R-HSA-8981373): SGLT1 co-transports Na+ with glucose and galactose, and basolateral GLUT2 releases hexoses into the blood. Glycolysis (R-HSA-70171): entirely cytosolic; two NAD+ are reduced to NADH per glucose; under anaerobic conditions or in cells lacking mitochondria NAD+ is regenerated by reducing pyruvate to lactate. Hexokinase reaction (R-HSA-70420): glucokinase and the three hexokinases catalyse an irreversible reaction; glucokinase occurs only in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, has a higher Km than the hexokinases, is less readily inhibited by its product and is thought to act as a glucose sensor coupled to insulin release; glucokinase mutations are associated with MODY2. Phosphofructokinase 1 (R-HSA-70467): irreversible under physiological conditions, allosterically regulated by ATP, citrate and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (R-HSA-9634600): its levels rise with insulin and fall with glucagon signalling; PKA phosphorylates PFKFB1. Pyruvate kinase (R-HSA-71670): essentially irreversible; isozymes L (liver) and R (red cells) come from PKLR, and PKLR mutations are associated with haemolytic anaemias. Pyruvate metabolism (R-HSA-70268): when oxygen is limiting, as in exercising muscle, or mitochondria are absent, as in red blood cells, NADH is reoxidised by reducing pyruvate to lactate, which is released into the blood, taken up mainly by the liver, oxidised to pyruvate and used for gluconeogenesis. Gluconeogenesis (R-HSA-70263): glucose synthesis from pyruvate consumes six high-energy phosphates, four from ATP and two from GTP. PDH complex (R-HSA-9861559): the mitochondrial complex converts pyruvate, CoA and NAD+ to acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. PDH regulation (R-HSA-204174): PDK1 to PDK4 inactivate the complex by phosphorylation and PDP1 and PDP2 reactivate it. Vitamin B1 metabolism (R-HSA-196819): Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is associated with thiamin deficiency in alcoholism. Citric acid cycle (R-HSA-71403): all reactions are mitochondrial; the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA is completely oxidised to CO2, yielding one GTP or ATP, three NADH and one FADH2. Citrate synthase (R-HSA-70975) and IDH3 (R-HSA-70967) are irreversible; IDH3 releases CO2, is activated by ADP and inhibited by NADH and high ATP; the OGDH reaction (R-HSA-71401) releases CO2; aconitase, succinyl-CoA ligase, fumarate hydratase and MDH2 are reversible, MDH2 being highly endergonic but pulled forward by the cycle; succinate dehydrogenase (R-HSA-70994) reduces ubiquinone, with FAD covalently bound to His-99 of SDHA. Respiratory electron transport (R-HSA-611105): energy is largely released in mitochondria; oxygen consumption depends on ADP availability; 2.5 ATP form per NADH electron pair and 1.5 per FADH2 pair; 10 NADH give 25 and 2 FADH2 give 3, 28 in all, plus 2 from the Krebs cycle and 2 from glycolysis, 32 per glucose in theory; the actual yield probably does not reach 32; the glycerol phosphate shuttle bypasses complex I, so 1.5 ATP form per cytosolic NADH, while malate-aspartate shuttle NADH enters at complex I. Statements not used, because they conflict with UniProt or with the arithmetic: R-HSA-611105 assigns 3 ATP to malate-aspartate shuttle NADH and swaps the overall equations of the two shuttles; R-HSA-71401 states that ATP and NADH enhance and Ca2+ and ADP decrease OGDH activity, the reverse of UniProt Q02218; R-HSA-204174 states that dichloroacetic acid inhibits PDH, whereas UniProt records it as an inhibitor of PDK1 to PDK3.
